title: What training does MSHA require for miners?
description: MSHA Part 46 and Part 48 miner training explained: new miner hours, 8 hour annual refresher, task training, training plans and Form 5000-23 records.
shortAnswer: The Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) requires mine operators to train every miner under an approved plan. Under 30 CFR Part 46, which covers sand, gravel and surface aggregate mines, new miners need at least 24 hours of training. Under Part 48, new underground miners need 40 hours before starting work and new surface miners 24 hours. Every miner needs at least 8 hours of annual refresher training, and task training before a new task.
keyTakeaways: Part 46 covers shell dredging, sand, gravel, surface stone, surface clay, colloidal phosphate and surface limestone mines. Part 48 covers underground mines (Subpart A) and all other surface mines and surface areas of underground mines (Subpart B).

New miner hours differ by part: 24 hours under Part 46 (4 before work, the rest within 90 days), 40 hours before work duties for underground miners under section 48.5, and 24 hours for surface miners under section 48.25.
Annual refresher training is at least 8 hours under sections 46.8, 48.8 and 48.28, and Part 46 requires it within 12 months of the previous session.
Training must be recorded and certified on MSHA Form 5000-23 or an equivalent form, and false certification is punishable under section 110(a) and (f) of the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act.
Training is conducted during normal working hours at the miner's normal rate of pay, with travel, meals and lodging reimbursed when it is held elsewhere.
regulator: Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA), US Department of Labor
appliesTo: Production operators and independent contractors at sand, gravel, surface stone, surface clay, colloidal phosphate, surface limestone and shell dredging operations (Part 46)
Operators of underground coal and metal and nonmetal mines (Part 48 Subpart A)
Operators of other surface mines, including surface coal mines, and surface areas of underground mines (Part 48 Subpart B)
Miners, including new miners, newly hired experienced miners, and miners reassigned to new tasks
Non-miners at a mine site, such as delivery drivers, office staff and vendors, who need site-specific hazard awareness or hazard training

sections.heading: Does Part 46 or Part 48 apply to a mine?

blocks.text: The commodity and the type of operation decide the part. [30 CFR Part 46](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-30/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-46) sets the mandatory training requirements for shell dredging, sand, gravel, surface stone, surface clay, colloidal phosphate and surface limestone mines. [30 CFR Part 48](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-30/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-48) covers everything else: Subpart A for underground mines, and Subpart B for surface mines and the surface areas of underground mines.

The two parts share a structure (new miner, experienced miner, task, annual refresher and hazard or site awareness training) but differ in hours, approval mechanics and record retention. A company that runs both an aggregate quarry and a surface coal operation will usually maintain two training plans and two sets of course outlines, which is where a [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) split by mine and part pays off.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects 30 CFR Parts 46 and 48 as published in the Electronic Code of Federal Regulations as at November 2026. Check the primary text before relying on any section number or hour requirement.

sections.heading: How many hours of new miner training are required?

blocks.text: New miner training is 24 hours under Part 46, 40 hours for new underground miners under section 48.5, and 24 hours for new surface miners under section 48.25. The timing rules are what separate the parts in practice.

items: **Part 46, section 46.5:** at least 4 hours before the miner begins work, covering a walkaround of the mine, hazard recognition including electrical hazards, emergency and evacuation procedures, task health and safety including HazCom, miners' statutory rights, lines of authority, and hazard reporting. Self-rescue and respiratory device training and first aid follow within 60 calendar days, and the balance of the 24 hours within 90 calendar days. Until the full 24 hours is complete, the new miner must work where an experienced miner can observe them.

**Part 48 underground, section 48.5:** at least 40 hours before the miner is assigned work duties, conducted in conditions that duplicate underground conditions as closely as practicable, with approximately 8 hours given at the minesite.

**Part 48 surface, section 48.25:** 24 hours, normally before work duties. The MSHA District Manager may allow part of it after assignment, but at least 8 hours must always be given first, and the remainder within 60 days.

blocks.text: Part 46 also lets a new miner who completed new miner training under section 46.5 or 48.25 within the previous 36 months, and who has under 12 months of surface mining experience, skip repeating the full course. They still need the before-work subjects in section 46.5(b).

sections.heading: What training do experienced miners and reassigned miners need?

blocks.text: Newly hired experienced miners need site orientation training before they start, and any miner moved to an unfamiliar task needs task training before performing it. Under section 46.6, a newly hired experienced miner receives the same seven before-work subjects as a new miner, plus self-rescue and respiratory device instruction within 60 calendar days where those devices are used.

Under section 48.6, experienced miner training applies to experienced miners who are newly employed, transferred to the mine, moving from surface to underground, or returning after an absence of more than 12 months, and must be completed before work duties. A miner returning to mining after an absence of 5 years or more must receive at least 8 hours.

Task training under section 46.7 must cover the health and safety aspects and safe work procedures of the task, chemical hazards and the HazCom program, and must be given before the miner performs the new task. It is not required where the miner has previous training or experience in the task and the operator observes that they can perform it safely. Section 48.7 lists categories, including mobile equipment, drilling, haulage and conveyor systems, roof and ground control machines, and blasting, where miners may not perform the new task until trained, unless trained and demonstrated safe operation within the preceding 12 months.

sections.heading: What must annual refresher training include, and when is it due?

blocks.text: Every miner must receive at least 8 hours of annual refresher training. Section 46.8 makes the deadline explicit: no later than 12 months after the miner begins work at the mine, and thereafter no later than 12 months after the previous annual refresher was completed. Sections 48.8 and 48.28 set the same 8 hour minimum for underground and surface miners.

Part 46 requires the refresher to include instruction on changes at the mine that could adversely affect miners' health or safety, and recommends subjects drawn from the equipment that has caused the most fatalities and serious injuries at covered mines: mobile equipment, conveyor systems, cranes, crushers, excavators and dredges. Part 48 prescribes course content, including mandatory health and safety standards related to the miner's tasks, transportation controls and communication systems, escape and emergency evacuation plans, ground control, and first aid.

The 12 month window under Part 46 is rolling, so a refresher completed late resets the next due date from its completion. Setting reminders against each miner's last completion date, rather than a single calendar month for the whole workforce, avoids gaps. The guide on [setting mandatory refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) covers rolling and fixed cycle approaches.

sections.heading: What must an MSHA training plan and instructor provide?

blocks.text: Both parts require an approved written training plan. Section 46.3 requires a written plan containing effective programs for new miners, newly hired experienced miners, new tasks, annual refresher training and site-specific hazard awareness training. Section 48.3 requires each underground mine operator to have an MSHA approved plan covering new miner, experienced miner, new task, annual refresher and hazard training.

Under section 46.4, each session must follow the written plan, be presented by a competent person, and be presented in a language the miners understand. Part 46 defines a competent person as someone designated by the operator who has the ability, training, knowledge or experience to train miners in their area of expertise, and who can both communicate the subject effectively and evaluate whether the training was effective.

That definition builds evaluation into the instructor role. An auditor reviewing a Part 46 program can reasonably ask how the competent person judged effectiveness, which links directly to [measuring training effectiveness](/guides/how-to-measure-training-effectiveness).

sections.heading: What records does MSHA require, and how long are they kept?

blocks.text: Operators must record and certify training on MSHA Form 5000-23 or a form containing the same information. Under section 46.9, the record must include the miner's printed full name, the type, duration and date of training, the name of the competent person who gave it, the mine or contractor identification number, and the statement "False certification is punishable under § 110(a) and (f) of the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act", signed by the person responsible for training under the plan.

Part 46 records for currently employed miners are kept for the duration of employment, except annual refresher records, which are kept for two years, and all records are kept for at least 60 calendar days after a miner leaves. Under section 48.9, certificates for currently employed miners are kept at the minesite for 2 years, or for 60 days after termination of employment, and a miner is entitled to copies when leaving.

Under sections 46.10 and 48.10, training must be conducted during normal working hours and paid at the miner's normal rate, with mileage, meals and lodging reimbursed for off-site training. See [preparing training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) and the wider picture for [energy and resources organizations](/industries/energy-resources).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models each mine's training plan as a framework of miner groups, tasks and site hazards, then links each task to the knowledge and observation points that show a miner can perform it safely. When a mine adds equipment or changes a task, the affected miners and the task training they need can be identified from the framework.

faqs.q: Can annual refresher training be split into shorter sessions?
faqs.a: The rules set a minimum of 8 hours of annual refresher training, and Part 46 requires a record to be made after each session of refresher training, which shows sessions can be split. The total must reach 8 hours within the 12 month period, and the certified record is provided to the miner on completion of the 8 hours.

faqs.q: Do truck drivers delivering to a quarry need MSHA training?
faqs.a: Customers and commercial over-the-road truck drivers who are not miners need site-specific hazard awareness training before exposure to mine hazards under section 46.11. Operators do not have to make Form 5000-23 records for non-miners but must be able to show the training was given, for example with handouts or visitor log entries.

Under Part 46, training must be presented by a competent person designated by the operator, in a language miners understand, and in line with the written plan. Operators can run their own programs or use state or federal agencies, associations, consultants and other providers, provided the training follows the approved plan.

faqs.q: What happens if a miner misses annual refresher training while away?
faqs.a: Under section 46.6(f), a miner who returns to the same mine after 12 months or less receives training on changes during the absence before starting work, and any missed annual refresher training must be provided no later than 90 calendar days after the miner begins work again.
